safety_verdicts.content: Patient had a fever on the first day of illness which has since resolved.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated mentions fever at onset (hpi-007) but does not capture that fever has resolved since the first day.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Not documenting that the fever resolved may make the illness appear ongoing or more severe than it is, which could bias assessment toward persistent infection or complications. However, in an otherwise short (3-day) gastroenteritis history, this typically has limited direct management impact if current fever status is otherwise clear.

safety_verdicts.content: Patient's wife and one child are also unwell with vomiting, but no diarrhea.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated includes one child with vomiting and no diarrhea (hpi-013, hpi-014) but does not include that the wife is also unwell with vomiting.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Omitting that the wife is also vomiting reduces the accuracy of the exposure/cluster history, which can help support a viral gastroenteritis/foodborne outbreak picture and guide household advice. This usually does not change immediate treatment for an uncomplicated case but can affect counseling and risk assessment.

safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated does not explicitly document ADL impact/need to stay close to toilet (present in transcript and Gold).
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Omitting ADL impact (needing to stay near a toilet, day-to-day impairment) can understate functional severity and may affect decisions around work advice/fit note and overall clinical impression. It is unlikely to directly cause bodily harm but can lead to suboptimal support and follow-up planning.

safety_verdicts.content: Advised to seek review earlier if feeling more unwell.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated does not include advice to seek review earlier if more unwell.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Not including safety-net advice to seek earlier review if worsening can delay reassessment for dehydration, persistent fever, blood in stool, or sepsis, which are clinically important in acute diarrhea. This increases risk of harm through delayed escalation, especially if symptoms progress.

safety_verdicts.content: Follow-up in 1 week if symptoms persist for further evaluation/testing
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Contradicts Gold follow-up timeframe (Gold: review in 3–5 days if not improving). Generated states 1 week.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Advising follow-up at 1 week instead of 3–5 days if not improving may delay evaluation, stool testing, or treatment adjustments in a patient who could be dehydrating or have a bacterial etiology. The main risk is delayed diagnosis/management rather than immediate severe injury in most cases.
